title: Grammaticalization of Motion Verbs into Directional Postpositions in Tangkhul
alternate_titles: Spatial Deixis and Path Markers in Tangkhul Verbal Syntax
subject: Syntax, Semantics & Grammaticalization
notes: Traces the diachronic evolution of lexical motion verbs (kava 'go', khura 'come', kashok 'exit') into directional aspect auxiliaries.
abstract: This paper investigates the grammaticalization pathways through which full lexical motion verbs in Tangkhul have developed into directional markers, telic aspectual affixes, and spatial postpositions. Drawing on connected texts spanning a century of documentation, we demonstrate that motion verbs specifying vertical axis (ascent/descent) and deictic orientation (centrifugal vs centripetal) systematically fuse with verbal stems to form complex path predicates.

sections.title: 1. Lexical Source Verbs & Deictic Trajectories
sections.content: Tangkhul distinguishes three basic deictic path vectors: (i) Centripetal movement toward speaker (-ung eina ungkaphung), (ii) Centrifugal movement away from speaker (-va eina vazatkasa), and (iii) Altitude-conditioned vectors: ascent uphill (-ka) and descent downhill (-tuk).

tangkhul_data.gloss: to arrive coming home toward speaker
to go away departing from speaker
to climb up out of a gorge onto peak

sections.title: 2. Verbal Serialisation & Affixation
sections.content: In serial verb constructions, the directional verb loses its independent nominal arguments and undergoes phonological reduction into an aspectual clitic. For instance, in 'a ot sa-va-ye' (He went off to do work), the auxiliary -va marks departure aspect rather than physical walking.

tangkhul_data.gloss: did and departed / went off doing

tangkhul_data.notes: Directional verb shok (exit) grammaticalized as telic resultative.

sections.title: 3. Typological Parallels in Tibeto-Burman
sections.content: The Tangkhul grammaticalization cline [Motion Verb -> Serial Verb -> Directional Affix -> Aspect Marker] directly mirrors paradigms observed in Qiang, Jingpho, and Lahu, providing evidence for areal Tibeto-Burman syntactic evolution.
